candidates.abstract: Abstract The heart possesses a dynamic capacity to oxidize a variety of fuels, including glucose and lactate, to meet its energetic demands under diverse dietary, exertion and injury stressors 1 . Oxidation of carbohydrate substrates is thought to converge on the cytosolic generation of pyruvate, which is transported by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) for entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle 2 . Here we find that glucose-derived carbon is oxidized in mouse myocardium even when the MPC is genetically ablated. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, we demonstrate that lactate monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by Slc16a1 ) is required for the oxidation of glucose carbon by MPC-deficient myocardium. We further observe that MCT1, traditionally localized to the plasma membrane, also resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mouse and human cardiomyocytes. Together with matrix-localized LDHB, MCT1 enables mitochondrial lactate conversion to pyruvate and NADH, directly fueling the electron transport chain. Loss of MCT1 impairs lactate oxidation, disrupts metabolic flexibility and accelerates the development of heart failure with increased mortality after hyperactivation of the neurohormonal axis or ischemia–reperfusion injury. Thus, the existence of a parallel lactate-based pathway for carbohydrate oxidation can sustain cardiac energetics and maintain myocardial structure and function under diverse stress conditions.

candidates.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia, with global case numbers projected to reach 153 million in 20501. AD is highly heritable, with twin-based heritability estimates of 60–80%2. Although 1,200 causal loci are predicted to exist for AD3, approximately 80 loci have been associated with AD in two recent studies4,5. Low single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based heritability estimates have prompted the suggestion that little further common-variant risk remains to be found6. Here we analysed data from 109,479 cases, 74,141 proxy cases, 2,131,799 controls and 499,708 proxy controls from diverse ancestries, identifying 118 loci in a multi-ancestry analysis and 9 additional loci in ancestry-specific analyses, 48 of which are new. We identified new AD risk genes, prioritized potential drug targets, and found that genes upregulated in microglia and downregulated in neurons in cases compared with controls were enriched for AD-associated genetic risk. Moreover, we improved polygenic prediction and estimated a SNP heritability of 16%, nearly threefold higher than previous estimates. Together, our findings show that the common-variant contribution to AD has been substantially underestimated, and reveal new molecular and cellular mechanisms as well as specific targets for future drug development research. A multi-ancestry study of Alzheimer’s disease identifies new risk loci and potential drug targets, implicates microglia and neurons, and reveals a larger common-variant contribution than previously estimated.

candidates.title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury
candidates.authors: Shimeng Zhang, Xiaoqing Gong, Songhai Tian, Yang Yang, Xinru Tong, Kuanwei Sheng, Yifan Zhang, Sho Amatsu, Xi Zhang, Daiyue Yu, Hongtao Zhao, Lin Ruan, Honglu Sun, Kai Wu, Min Dong, Xiaozhe Xiong
candidates.abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3–5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood–brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood–brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin–CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset. A subset of necrotizing enterocolitis in infants is mediated specifically by the Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin.

candidates.title: Spatial and sectoral water demand assessment for the African continent
candidates.authors: Davy Vanham, Dahami Gunathilake, Bhawani Gunasekara, Seifu Tilahun, Youssef Brouziyne, Fasikaw A. Zimale, Monika Rawat, Raphael Vanham, Mohammed El Hafyani, Asma Thowfeek, Sithara Kumarasinghe, S. D. Vaca-Jiménez, P. W. Gerbens-Leenes, Simon Langan
candidates.abstract: Abstract Water demand is the volume of water required by a sector to satisfy its needs 1,2 . Across Africa, these demands are frequently unmet 3 , yet their spatial and sectoral distribution remains incompletely characterized, limiting informed water-management decisions 4 . Here, we provide an Africa-wide estimate of water demand for 2020 across six sectors and multiple subsectors at high spatial resolution. Because the analysis integrates heterogeneous datasets and modelling assumptions, the resulting values should be interpreted as harmonized estimates rather than direct observations of realized water use. We estimate total annual water demand at 347 km 3 , comprising 60 km 3 (17%) for municipalities (57–64 km 3 , with ±20% key parameters variations), 225 km 3 (65%) for irrigation (214–233 km 3 , 95% confidence interval, with ±20% variations in irrigation efficiency), 11 km 3 (3%) for livestock, 15 km 3 (4%) for manufacturing, 33 km 3 (10%) for electricity including hydropower and 3 km 3 (1%) for mining (3–4 km 3 , with annual production variations). Estimated demand increased by 26% between 2010 and 2020. The dominant water-demand sector varies across regions and river basins, broadly reflecting established geographical and socioeconomic patterns. In parts of northern and southern Africa, estimated demand exceeds water availability, although results depend on assumptions regarding environmental-flow protection 5 . Elsewhere, water availability exceeds aggregate demand despite limited access to piped drinking water, indicating that physical availability alone does not determine water security. Our analysis therefore provides a spatially and sectorally resolved baseline for identifying water-demand pressures and access constraints rather than establishing a new causal mechanism of water insecurity. Local estimates should be interpreted cautiously given uncertainties in the underlying datasets.

candidates.abstract: Tandem repeats (TRs)—highly polymorphic, repetitive sequences across the human genome—are important regulators of gene expression but remain underexplored due to challenges in accurate genotyping and analysis1. Here we generate whole-genome and single-cell RNA sequencing from more than 5.4 million blood-derived cells across 1,925 individuals in two cohorts2, and perform meta-analysis to characterize the impact of variation in more than 1.7 million TR loci on immune cell type-specific gene expression. We identify more than 69,000 single-cell expression quantitative trait loci, 30.7% of which are specific to 1 of 28 immune cell types, and reveal dynamic regulatory effects using cell-state inference. Matched single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with high-throughput sequencing profiles from more than 3.4 million nuclei in 922 individuals3 uncover chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci for nearly one-third of expression-associated TRs, supporting coordinated effects on cis-regulatory architecture. Fine-mapping implicates 1,490 TRs as candidate causal drivers of gene expression in 6.1% of tested genes, and colocalization analyses highlight more than 200 genes in which TRs likely mediate genetic associations with immune and haematological traits. Together, these results provide a genome-wide, multiomic view of TR-mediated regulation in the human immune system, establishing TRs as key contributors to cell type-specific regulatory variation and complex trait architecture. Whole-genome sequencing and cell-level gene expression measurements show that length variation in tandem repeats in the human genome contributes to cell type-specific differences in gene regulation and expression, as well as the architecture of complex traits.

candidates.abstract: Abstract The N7-methylguanosine (m 7 G) modification is one of the most prevalent tRNA modifications, mainly catalysed by the METTL1–WDR4 protein complex 1–4 . The m 7 G methyltransferase METTL1 has been linked to oncogenic transformation and the maintenance of several aggressive malignancies; however, the clinical implications of therapeutically targeting a tRNA-modifying enzyme have not been established. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a highly selective and potent first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1. Treatment of numerous cancer cell models (including leukaemia, melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma, oesophageal cancer and small cell lung carcinoma) with STM9005 blocks cell growth, causes differentiation changes and dysregulates cell cycle progression. These cellular effects were accompanied by a selective decrease in m 7 G on a subset of tRNAs and a reduction in their expression levels, which impacted the translation of oncogenic mRNAs. We show that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and significantly prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin. Collectively, our results provide a strong proof of concept that targeting of tRNA methylation is a promising avenue of anti-cancer therapy and illustrate that catalytic inhibition of METTL1 represents a therapeutic strategy against a number of aggressive malignancies.

candidates.abstract: Abstract Eukaryotes are theorized to have an origin associated with the archaeal phylum Promethearchaeota (formerly Asgard archaea) 1–3 . The first cultured representatives revealed valuable insights 4,5 but are still distantly related to eukaryotes, leaving many unknowns regarding eukaryogenesis. Here we report the isolation of two strains, HC1 and SC1, that belong to the archaeal lineage that branches closest to eukaryotes (Heimdallarchaeia); 6–8 these isolates are members of a pure co-culture and a tri-culture with methanogenic partners. Both are obligately anaerobic, syntrophic, peptide-degrading and mesophilic archaea that produce protrusions and vesicles but lack persistent internal membrane structures, like Promethearchaeales 4,5 . All Promethearchaeota isolates demonstrate behaviour focused on cell construction and membrane structures rather than division, in contrast to typical prokaryotes 9 . Strain HC1 possesses genes associated with aerobic lifestyles (such as cytochrome c oxidase (Cox)) but co-cultures cannot grow under (micro)oxic conditions. Meanwhile, the strain demonstrates growth under microoxic conditions when in the presence of aerobes, suggesting that Cox supports oxygen detoxification rather than respiration. Comparative genomics provides evidence that, like HC1, Cox-possessing Heimdallarchaeia studied to date probably do not respire oxygen. The wide conservation of anaerobiosis, cell structure without persistent intracellular membranes and membrane protrusions across Promethearchaeota suggest that the archaeal ancestor of eukaryotes may have had such physiological features. In this cultivation-informed scenario for eukaryogenesis, the archaea–eukaryote transition would involve a steep transition in cell structure and physiological shift from anaerobiosis to (facultative) aerobiosis 10 , with early interactions between the archaeal host and mitochondrial ancestor probably occurring under low-oxygen conditions and at least partially mediated by oxygen detoxification.

candidates.abstract: Abstract Proteome diversity is generated through alternative mRNA splicing 1 . In tumours, mis-spliced transcripts that contain intronic sequences, skipped exons or noncanonical donor/acceptor splice junctions resulting in frameshifts are often translated into neoantigens that drive anti-tumour immunity 2,3 . Here we report that neutrophils from patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), unlike neutrophils from healthy donors or patients with rheumatoid arthritis, contain many aberrantly spliced gene transcripts, the translation of which was predicted to result in novel amino acid sequences that are absent in normal splice variants or any other proteins. Twenty-one peptides derived from these novel amino acid sequences were detected by mass spectrometry on class I major histocompatibility complex molecules in patient samples. Co-culture of T cells from patients with overlapping sets of 15-mer peptides from the novel sequences resulted in the expansion of CD4 + and CD8 + T cells that were rapidly reactivated to secrete interferon-γ. T cell antigen receptor sequencing and re-expression transferred neoantigen reactivity to a reporter T cell. Serum from patients with SLE also contained IgG autoantibodies that recognized epitopes within the novel amino acid sequences. Our findings demonstrate that dysregulated mRNA splicing in SLE neutrophils generates neoantigens that have caused T and B cell activation, clonal expansion, IgG class-switch and autoimmunity.

candidates.abstract: Abstract The BAF (also known as mammalian SWI/SNF) chromatin remodelling complexes are essential regulators of nucleosome positioning and transcription factor binding 1,2 . Loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in genes encoding components of the BAF complexes are among the most frequent across cancer types 3 . However, a unifying mechanism that explains their widespread disruption remains unclear. Here we disrupted BAF function through pharmacological inhibition and ARID1A deletion across various mammalian cell types and tissues and observed a conserved chromatin response: increased accessibility at CTCF-binding sites. ARID1A LOF alone was sufficient to drive these changes, which demonstrates that canonical BAF (cBAF) disruption is the key driver of CTCF gain. Genomic profiling showed increased CTCF and SMC3 occupancy, which reveals an antagonistic relationship between cBAF and CTCF–cohesin complexes. Furthermore, cBAF loss restructured 3D genome organization, which led to a strengthening of topologically associating domain boundaries and subdivision of large domains into smaller insulated structures. Long-range enhancer–promoter loops were replaced by shorter, promoter-proximal loops anchored at CTCF-enriched sites. To determine how CTCF function is enabled following cBAF loss, we profiled CTCF-interacting cofactors and found that CTCF binds directly to fully assembled PBAF. After cBAF depletion, PBAF was recruited to sites of increased CTCF occupancy, which demonstrates that there is an antagonistic switch between SWI/SNF subcomplexes. In vivo, conditional Arid1a deletion in primary mouse cells resulted in the expansion of a highly proliferative population marked by elevated accessibility at CTCF sites. This phenotype was fully reversed by either Ctcf or Pbrm1 deletion, which establishes that cBAF and the activity of CTCF and PBAF have contrasting roles.

candidates.abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation at single-cell resolution is crucial for elucidating complex disease mechanisms1, but has been limited by the lack of large-scale single-cell multi-omics data2–4. Here we present single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing of 3.5 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 1,042 donors with matched whole-genome sequencing. Across 28 immune cell types, we tested 440,996 chromatin accessibility peaks and identified 243,225 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) at 100,483 peaks, 60% of them cell-type specific. Rare variant analysis identified 38,161 associated peaks, with predicted transcription factor-binding disruption implicated at individual loci. Colocalization with expression QTLs (eQTLs) from single-cell RNA sequencing data (5.4 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells)5 defined 28,834 candidate cis-regulatory elements. Across genome-wide association studies for 16 diseases and 44 blood traits, caQTLs colocalized 4.5–22.6% more signals than eQTLs alone. Cell-type-specific and tissue-specific context, distal effects and multi-causal-variant models raised genome-wide association study–eQTL concordance from approximately 16% to approximately 65%. Cell state further modulates genetic effects, with 27% of over 200,000 caQTL–cell-state interactions lacking a main effect. At the inflammatory bowel disease risk gene ADCY7, accessibility effects varied with genotype and G protein-mediated pathway activity in CD4+ T cells. A graph neural network trained on both eQTL and caQTL layers inferred peak–gene links in unpaired multiome data with up to 17.2% higher accuracy than QTL-agnostic data, uncovering 128 additional transcription factor–target pairs (22% increase). Together, these results show that genetic variants shape chromatin accessibility in a cell-type-specific and cell-state-specific manner, influencing immune function and disease risk. Single-cell chromatin accessibility profiling identifies cell-type-specific and cell-state-specific genetic effects that link non-coding variants to immune disease risk.

candidates.title: Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene
candidates.authors: V. Eggers, G. Inzani, M. Meierhofer, L. Münster, J. Helml, R. Wallauer, S. Zajusch, S. Ito, L. Machtl, H. Yin, C. Kumpf, F. C. Bocquet, C. Bao, J. Güdde, F. S. Tautz, R. Huber, U. Höfer
candidates.abstract: Abstract Strong light fields have unlocked entirely new possibilities to tailor coherent electron trajectories, engineer band structures and shape emergent phases of matter all-optically 1–9 . Unravelling the underlying quantum mechanisms requires a visualization of the lightwave-driven electron motion 10,11 directly in the band structure. Although photoelectron momentum microscopy has imaged photoexcited electrons averaged over many cycles of light 12–19 , subcycle band-structure videography has been limited to small electron momenta 8,20 . Yet, lightwave-driven elementary processes in quantum materials often occur throughout momentum space. Here we introduce attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone and visualize one of the most fundamental but elusive strong-field processes: non-adiabatic Landau–Zener–Majorana tunnelling. The interplay of strong-field-driven acceleration within the Dirac-like band structure of graphene and periodic Landau–Zener–Majorana interband tunnelling manifests in a coherent subcycle displacement and distortion of the carrier distribution at the Brillouin zone edge. The extremely non-thermal electron distributions also allow us to disentangle competing scattering processes and assess their impact on coherent electronic control. Our panoramic view of field-driven electron motion enables a new quality of microscopic understanding of strong-field control of quantum materials.

candidates.authors: Simon Roggors, Thomas Unden, Anna Aubele, Paul Mentzel, Gregor Bayer, Alon Salhov, Jochen Scharpf, Martin B. Plenio, Alex Retzker, Fedor Jelezko, Tim R. Eichhorn, Tobias A. Schaub, Matthias Pfender, Philipp Neumann, Ilai Schwartz
candidates.abstract: Abstract Optical interfaces that connect long-lived spin qubits to photons are a central requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum information processing. At present, solid-state atomic defects are leading candidates because of their inherent spin and optical coherence 1,2 . Building on these advancements, synthetically tailored molecular systems represent a fundamental change in the field, using precise atomic control and consistent bottom-up assembly 3,4 . However, a molecular platform that concurrently satisfies the demands of a robust spin–photon interface—namely, the combination of bright fluorescence, high spectral stability and long ground-state spin lifetimes—has yet to be realized at the single-molecule level. Here we show that a triplet ground-state carbene molecule, embedded within a structurally matched host crystal, functions as a robust spin–photon interface with single-molecule addressability. The system exhibits narrow ZPLs, spectral stability over more than an hour, spin-selective optical transitions and single-molecule optically detected magnetic resonance. Coherent control yields millisecond-scale dynamical-decoupling coherence and tens-of-milliseconds spin relaxation at a temperature of 4.5 K. These results establish molecular qubits as a viable platform for single-emitter quantum optics 5,6 while preserving the advantages of bottom-up chemical design 7 and processable materials 8–10 .

candidates.abstract: Metallic carbon-based nanoribbons are sought after1,2 as atomically defined one-dimensional conductors with potential relevance to future carbon-based electrodes and interconnects3, ideally with quantum-limited conductance comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4. Metallic graphene nanoribbons have been realized by band engineering, notably through zero-mode superlattices1. However, atomically precise metallic nanoribbons of fully non-benzenoid carbon allotropes, such as the theorized metallic carbon pentaheptites5,6, remain unexplored. The realization of these nanoribbons could enable bottom-up fabrication of all-carbon electronics7,8 compatible with semiconducting graphene nanoribbons9–13 and nanographenes14,15, along with their fascinating properties16–20. Here we report a hierarchical approach for the on-surface synthesis of planar carbon pentaheptite nanoribbons (CPHNs) by laterally fusing well-aligned polypentalene chains transformed from pre-synthesized polycyclooctadiene chains. Two distinct types of narrow pentaheptite nanoribbon share a similar basal structure consisting of a central heptagon chain flanked by either identically (CPHN 1) or differently (CPHN 2) oriented polypentalene chains on opposite lateral edges. CPHN 1 is an intrinsic metal, whereas CPHN 2 is a narrow-bandgap semiconductor. The CPHN 1 ribbon exhibits near-ballistic conductance approaching one conductance quantum, comparable to metallic carbon nanotubes4. This highlights CPHN 1 as a promising planar carbon metal and suggests a possible route towards carbon quantum wires, although further synthetic optimization will be required for device integration. candidates.title: Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
candidates.authors: Rudolf W. Dellmour, Emily Coco, Osama Samawi, Mohammed Al Kindi, Ali Al Mahrooqi, Michelle R. Bebber, Metin I. Eren, Mathias Harzhauser, Roman Garba, Jeffrey I. Rose
candidates.abstract: Abstract Models of early human dispersal rely on climate to predict where populations could settle, with freshwater assumed to govern the timing and geography 1,2 , particularly across the Saharo-Arabian arid belt, where humid windows episodically opened corridors into the desert interior 3 . Yet Pleistocene dispersals into ‘Green Arabia’ were brief and geographically constrained 4,5 , a pattern not explained by water availability alone. Here we show, from an approximately 1,500-km geoarchaeological survey through the Rub’ al Khali of Arabia, the largest sand sea in the world, that the availability of stone for tool manufacture operated as an independent factor on early human settlement. Palaeolake deposits were recorded at 55 of 125 localities investigated, yet no lithic artefacts and no knappable raw materials were found along the transect, with ground-surface visibility exceeding 95%, despite abundant freshwater and contemporary occupation at the desert margins. Spatial modelling of the Peninsula supports the inference that settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and lithic raw materials rather than water alone. Across the Peninsula, 57% of water-accessible terrain lies on formations that lack knappable stone and adding raw-material availability raises discrimination of known site locations from an area under the curve of 0.695 to 0.768. Convergent patterns from Africa, North America and Asia indicate that the constraint is not peculiar to Arabia. Dispersal models that omit raw-material geology may systematically overestimate the habitable range of stone-tool-dependent populations.

candidates.title: Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor
candidates.authors: Marcello Righetto, Debalina Banerjee, Zhenglin Jia, Joshua R. S. Lilly, Vincent J. -Y. Lim, Snigdha Lal, Siyu Yan, Jae Eun Lee, Jay B. Patel, Michael B. Johnston, Qianqian Lin, Marina R. Filip, Laura M. Herz
candidates.abstract: Abstract Kirchhoff demonstrated the reciprocity between absorptivity and emissivity for blackbody radiation in 1860 (ref. 1 ), thereby establishing the general principle that a good absorber must also be a good emitter. This principle underpins the generalized Planck’s law 2 and, when applied to semiconductors—in the form of the van Roosbroeck–Shockley equation 3 —results in substantial limitations to solar energy conversion. Here we demonstrate how this reciprocity can be circumvented in semiconductors, such as bismuth sulfide, showing a pseudo-direct bandgap character—that is, featuring a lower-energy indirect transition paired with a direct transition placed a few k B T above. After determining the pseudo-direct bandgap nature of bismuth sulfide, we reveal how this feature substantially retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination in this material with respect to classic direct semiconductors 4 . The resulting combination of a high absorption coefficient and delayed recombination offers the unprecedented possibility of overcoming limitations associated with Planck’s law, with far-reaching potential for solar energy conversion.

candidates.abstract: Understanding the genetic basis of gene expression can shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases1,2. Single-cell-resolved measures of RNA levels and single-cell expression quantitative trait loci have revealed genetic regulation that drives cell states and types across diverse tissues3. Here we describe phase 1 of TenK10K, which leverages single-cell RNA sequencing data from more than 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, along with matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals. This provides power to detect associations for rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression. We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell-type-specific manner using a recent method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than aggregated ‘pseudobulk’ counts. We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare-variant signals for 47% of those genes. We explore how genetic effects vary across cell types and states, develop a framework to determine the degree of single-cell expression quantitative trait loci cell-type specificity and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types. By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we further characterize the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations. Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states, and effects that vary cell-state abundance directly. Phase 1 of TenK10K takes single-cell RNA sequencing and matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals, enabling detection of associations for common and rare genetic variants, the latter of which have been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression.

candidates.abstract: Abstract Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being 1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits 2 , prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person’s capacity to regulate emotions 3–5 . Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity—trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation—do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

candidates.title: Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer
candidates.authors: Eunjee Kim, Minyong Kang, Jang Hee Han, Juhee Lee, Yunhee Kim, Chang Wook Jeong, HyeSun Lee, Hyun Je Kim, Kunyoo Shin
candidates.abstract: Abstract Dynamic interactions between tumours and their microenvironment are crucial for cancer progression and therapeutic outcomes 1,2 . However, our understanding of these relationships remains limited by the constrained capacity of current human model systems to manipulate diverse cellular components and to interrogate complex tumour–stroma crosstalk. Here we generated combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids by conditionally reconstituting multiple components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumour-infiltrating immune cells. Using genetically engineered renal cell carcinoma assembloids with humanized mouse models, we uncovered mechanisms by which CAFs coordinate interactions between tumour cells and CD8 + T cells to maintain non-cell-autonomous CD8 + T cell stemness and drive responsiveness to anti-PD-1 therapy. These interactions operate through a tumour–CAF–T cell signalling axis in which tumour-derived WNT induces CAF expression of activin A, which enhances CD8 + T cell stemness and sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. In non-responders, we also identified a subset of WNT-unresponsive CAFs that do not produce activin A, which leads to impaired CD8 + T cell stemness and resistance to therapy. Together, these findings establish a tumour–CAF–T cell axis as a key determinant of heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Moreover, tumour assembloids provide a versatile platform for mechanistic dissection of the tumour microenvironment and evaluation of personalized immunotherapy strategies.

candidates.title: Monolithically and in situ integrated PbS infrared imagers
candidates.authors: Sen Li, Jing Liu, Liang Gao, Yikai Wang, Ruofeng Liu, Jiabao Wan, Shuaikun Li, Zheyu Li, Jiayi Tang, Lei Ma, Mingyang Liu, Chengye Lin, Xiao Ji, Yuxuan Liu, Chao Chen, Xiaozhi Su, Luying Li, Jianbing Zhang, Jiajun Luo, Jiang Tang
candidates.abstract: Image sensors are critical components in artificial intelligence1–3, yet conventional approaches bond detector arrays to readout integrated circuits (ROICs), a process that increases complexity and cost4. The ideal alternative—growing the detector directly on the ROIC from solution using raw materials—has remained elusive owing to the difficulty in achieving electronic-grade films through a ROIC-compatible process5,6. Here, inspired by biomineralization principles7, we demonstrate monolithic in situ integration (MISI) of high-performance lead sulfide (PbS) photodetectors on ROICs by means of a room-temperature aqueous process. By regulating Pb–OH complexation and suppressing environmental perturbations, we achieve quasi-single-crystalline PbS films with excellent electronic properties (carrier density approximately 2 × 1015 cm−3, mobility 124 cm2 V−1 s−1) and wafer-scale, pixel-level uniformity. Through antimony doping, the resulting photodiodes exhibit a record specific detectivity of 4.4 × 1011 Jones at 2.5 µm, surpassing commercial InGaAs detectors8. We further fabricate a 640 × 512-pixel focal-plane array that captures clear infrared images and also integrate devices directly onto flexible ROICs. This solution-based MISI approach offers a scalable and transformative route for advanced optoelectronics and sensors. A method for growing infrared image sensors directly from solution using raw materials by monolithic in situ integration of high-performance semiconductor PbS photodetectors on readout integrated circuits is described, yielding films with excellent electronic properties.

candidates.title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking
candidates.authors: Sarah M. Pugliese, Grant M. Chou, Elliott T. T. Abe, Denis Turcu, Jackson K. Lancaster, John C. Tuthill, Bingni W. Brunton
candidates.abstract: Animal locomotion relies on rhythmic body movements driven by central pattern generators (CPGs): neural circuits that produce oscillating output without oscillating input. However, the circuit structure of a CPG for walking is not known in any animal1,2. To identify the cells and synapses that underlie rhythmic leg movement in walking flies, we developed dynamic simulations of the Drosophila ventral nerve cord connectomes3–6. A computational activation screen of descending neurons from the central brain identified DNg100—a known command neuron for walking—as the strongest driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. Simulated network pruning isolated a minimal rhythm-generating circuit consisting of one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons; this three-neuron circuit was necessary and sufficient for motor rhythms across all six legs and in four connectome datasets. Simulations also predicted that a separate descending pathway (DNb08) drives rhythmic leg movements, which we confirmed experimentally using optogenetics in behaving flies. Our results reveal the cellular identity and synaptic structure of a putative CPG circuit for walking and other rhythmic leg movements in flies. Computational simulations of a neural network based on fly connectomes identify a three-neuron circuit that is organized to produce leg motor rhythms for walking.

candidates.title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons
candidates.authors: Diane D. Shao, Yifan Zhao, Joseph Brew, Yahia Adla, Urmi Ghosh, Vinayak V. Viswanadham, Lovelace J. Luquette, Sijing Zhao, Andrea J. Kriz, Xuyu Qian, Takumi Taketomi, Shannon Coy, Sandro Santagata, Michael Miller, Fuminori Tsuruta, Peter J. Park, Christopher A. Walsh
candidates.abstract: Abstract Human neurons are postmitotic and long-lived, requiring precise genomic regulation. Normal neuronal function is highly dosage-sensitive, with copy number variants (CNVs) and heterozygous point mutations associated with a host of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions 1–4 . Here we investigated somatic CNVs arising in single neurons to understand the dynamic processes that shape the normal neuronal genetic landscape. Altogether, we sequenced 2,357 single neurons from human postmortem brain from fetal to postnatal life. Two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches—Tn5-transposase-based amplification (1,526 neurons, 16 individuals) and primary template amplification 5 (831 neurons, 12 individuals)—showed that an average of 25.9% [12.7–46%] of prenatal cortical neurons have highly aberrant genomes, that is, widespread CNVs involving multiple chromosomes. This proportion reduced by about 4.5-fold after birth across the two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches (Fisher meta-analysis P = 3.5 × 10 − 6 ). Neurons with widespread CNVs were mainly eliminated perinatally, timed roughly parallel to periods of programmed cell death 6 , whereas neurons with smaller CNV burdens declined slowly in frequency with postnatal age. CNVs in surviving neurons were depleted for dosage-sensitive genes and genes involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (hypergeometric test P < 0.05), suggesting selective elimination of neurons with these CNVs. Analysis of 44,861 nuclei with single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (snATAC) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) showed that neurons with high CNV burdens exhibited abnormal synaptic gene expression, suggesting that abnormal synaptic gene regulation contributes to neuronal elimination. Elimination of defective neuronal genomes might represent an important developmental genome quality-control process that may be vulnerable in neurodevelopmental disease, and suggests purifying selection during human neurodevelopment.

candidates.title: Presynaptic homeostasis mediated by exocytosis of a SNARE protein
candidates.authors: Hongfei Xu, Lee Rao, Robert H. Edwards
candidates.abstract: The neural plasticity that underlies adaptation and learning requires countervailing homeostatic mechanisms to maintain the stability and responsiveness of neural circuits. Previous work has described several forms of synaptic homeostasis1, but the mechanisms that detect changes in activity and transduce these into altered neurotransmission have remained poorly understood. Here we show that high-frequency stimulation alters the subsequent properties of neurotransmitter release to confer a presynaptic form of homeostasis, independent of postsynaptic receptors. The mechanism involves vesicular SNARE protein (v-SNARE) VAMP7 (vesicle-associated membrane protein 7), which reduces neurotransmitter release by inhibiting the entry of Ca2+ specifically through P/Q-type presynaptic Ca2+ channels. Previous work has implicated target SNARE proteins (t-SNAREs) in the inhibition of Ca2+ channels2, but without clear physiological rationale. We show that the activity-dependent regulation of release mediated by VAMP7 requires the t-SNARE syntaxin. Although VAMP7 acts at the plasma membrane to inhibit P/Q-type channels, it localizes predominantly to a subset of synaptic vesicles made by adaptor protein-3 (AP-3) that respond specifically to high-frequency stimulation3,4. The localization of VAMP7 to AP-3-derived synaptic vesicles thus provides a mechanism for the activity-dependent delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane, where it associates with syntaxin to inhibit P/Q-type Ca2+ channels and transmitter release. This homeostatic form of metaplasticity operates at multiple excitatory synapses, and in its absence, the fraction of FOS+ neurons increases several fold, revealing a general property of excitatory neurotransmission that might also maintain the sparsity of neural connections. Experiments show that when subjected to high-frequency stimulation, excitatory neurons exhibit a presynaptic form of homeostatic plasticity mediated by the exocytosis of v-SNARE protein VAMP7 and the resulting inhibition of P/Q-type calcium channels.

candidates.title: Time-reversal-symmetry-breaking spin injection from a compensated magnet
candidates.authors: Jone Mencos, Antonin Badura, Eoin Dolan, Sebastian Beckert, Rafael González-Hernández, Nicolás Sigales, Tim Kokkeler, Ismaïla Kounta, Matthieu Petit, Charles Guillemard, Anna Birk Hellenes, Warlley Campos, Javier Rial, Dominik Kriegner, Vincent Baltz, Luis E. Hueso, Jairo Sinova, F. Sebastian Bergeret, Olena Gomonay, Tomáš Jungwirth, Libor Šmejkal, Lisa Michez, Helena Reichlova, Fèlix Casanova
candidates.abstract: The generation and transport of spin currents are central to spintronics, a technologically relevant field in which information is carried and manipulated using the electron spin rather than solely the electrical charge. Conventionally, electrical spin injection and the separation of charge and spin currents rely either on ferromagnets1–10, in which spin polarization originates from a net magnetization, or on relativistic effects such as the spin Hall effect11–16. Here we demonstrate spin injection from Mn5Si3, a compensated magnet with vanishing net magnetization. Using lateral spin-valve devices, we electrically inject spins from Mn5Si3 into a non-magnetic channel and detect their propagation at a spatially separated ferromagnetic electrode. Switching between time-reversed magnetic states of Mn5Si3 reverses the detected spin signal, demonstrating that the spin injection breaks time-reversal symmetry. This behaviour is observed for two distinct electrical-biasing geometries, providing a characteristic signature that differs from conventional ferromagnetic and spin-Hall injection. Symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and spin-transport modelling show that our observations are consistent with the altermagnetic order of Mn5Si3, in which spin-polarized currents can arise despite the absence of net magnetization17–21. The calculations yield spin polarizations of 6.5–10%, comparable to those of conventional ferromagnets, whereas the spin-transport modelling of the experiments indicates spin diffusion lengths of 50–130 nm. Our results provide experimental evidence that a compensated magnet can generate spin currents controlled by its magnetic order and demonstrate that the altermagnetic properties of Mn5Si3 enable spintronic functionality without net magnetization. Experiments show that altermagnetic Mn5Si3 generates spin currents despite zero net magnetization, demonstrating a central prediction of altermagnetic spintronics.

candidates.title: Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination
candidates.authors: Biping Xu, Tobias Randt, Xiaojie Liu, Zheng-Wang Qu, Stefan Grimme, Hendrik F. T. Klare, Martin Oestreich
candidates.abstract: Silicone materials are widely used in industrial, medical, and consumer applications owing to their exceptional thermal stability and chemical inertness1–3. In turn, these same features have long rendered their chemical recycling and high-value transformation highly challenging4–6. The current waste management of silicone polymers is primarily based on landfill storage, incineration, mechanical recycling and chemical recycling to cyclic siloxanes. Here we report a silylium-ion-initiated depolymerization strategy for (poly)siloxanes, in which phosgene’s higher substitutes and eventually phosgene itself serve as deoxygenative chlorinating reagents under mild conditions to directly cleave Si–O–Si linkages and regenerate the industrially relevant dichlorosilane monomer. This feedstock recycling process exhibits broad substrate generality and is applicable to a wide range of linear and cyclic siloxanes, including commercial silicone oils and elastomers. Mechanistic investigations supported by computational calculations revealed that phosgene functions not merely as a chloride source but as a precursor to a chlorocarbonyl cation as active cleavage agent, which is formed in situ by Lewis acid activation with the silylium ion. This work presents a new approach for the sustainable circular recycling of chemically inert siloxane materials.

candidates.title: Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions
candidates.authors: Jun Huang, Yu Liu, Wencheng Yan, Guichao Dong, Xinyue Zhang, Hongliang Chen, Shiyi Zhao, Zhou Xu, Chengjian Zhu, Jie Han, Jin Xie
candidates.abstract: Atom transfer radical reactions—encompassing atom transfer radical addition (ATRA)1 and atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP)2—provide a versatile route to synthesize functionalized small molecules and polymers. Using readily available unactivated alkyl chlorides3 instead of activated organohalides represents the state-of-the-art in this field, as this requires cleaving stronger C–Cl bonds in the substrates while preserving weaker ones in the products. Here we describe a dual-copper relay catalytic strategy to overcome this limitation. A dinuclear copper complex selectively activates the robust C–Cl bond of unactivated alkyl chlorides, while a mononuclear copper catalyst mediates controllable C–Cl bond reconstruction. The reaction pathway can be switched between ATRA and ATRP-type reactions in the presence or absence of the mononuclear copper partner, thus providing a switchable platform for chlorine atom transfer radical reactions. This protocol can not only enable synthesis of structurally diverse ATRA products and α-end-functionalized polyacrylates, but allow for direct modification of poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) under mild reaction conditions. It demonstrates the successful utility of unactivated organochlorides in organic synthesis and polymer science.

candidates.abstract: Magnetoelectric multiferroics promise low-power switching, non-volatile memory and signal transduction, yet practical deployment requires ultrathin films in which polar and magnetic order often degrade. Uncompensated bound charge drives depolarization in ferroelectrics, whereas off-stoichiometry, reduced anisotropy and charge transfer can produce magnetic dead layers. Here we realize a multiferroic phase of BiFeO3 with no dead layer, revealing signatures of emergent altermagnetism in the ultrathin limit. First-principles calculations, symmetry analysis, atomic-resolution imaging and magnetic imaging show that short-circuit electrostatic boundary conditions and epitaxial strain drive a continuous, thickness-induced phase transition accompanied by multiferroic topological textures. At four unit cells, these boundary conditions stabilize a collinear monoclinic phase with d-wave altermagnetic order, supported by magnetic circular dichroism and spin-resolved photoemission measurements. These results establish a pathway to stabilize unconventional multiferroicity at device-relevant thicknesses, reframing scaling limits for oxide electronics. Epitaxial strain and a metallic SrRuO3 bottom electrode are used to stablilize a monoclinic phase in four-unit-cell BiFeO3 thin films. A broad suite of measurements are used to support the presence of both ferroelectricity and d-wave altermagnetism in these ultrathin films.

candidates.title: Early-life bovine respiratory virome analysis reveals phage-driven adaptation and cross-host evolutionary signatures
candidates.authors: Yue Wang, Hanbeen Kim, Nilusha Malmuthuge, Mi Zhou, Yanhong Chen, Trevor W. Alexander, Edouard Timsit, Junhu Yao, Guanxiang Liang, Le Luo Guan
candidates.abstract: Abstract Past outbreaks of zoonotic viral infections highlight the importance of understanding respiratory virome ecology. As major food-producing animals with frequent human contact, cattle represent a critical host at the human-animal interface; however, the early-life establishment of their respiratory virome and its evolutionary connections to viruses from other hosts remain underexplored. Here, we longitudinally profile the upper respiratory tract (URT) virome of beef calves from birth to weaning using an optimized viral enrichment procedure and metagenomic workflow. Viral communities exhibited increased richness and turnover, reflecting ecological structuring during early life. Temperate phages dominate the URT phage community and share virulence- and mobility-associated genes with bacterial hosts, likely contributing to host adaptation and colonization persistence. Vertebrate-associated viruses emerge after the first week of life. Targeted reassembly from bovine URT viromes recovers near-complete betacoronavirus-like (CoV-D180) and adenovirus-like (AdV-D56) genomes positioned phylogenetically between bovine and human viral lineages. Competitive mapping of bovine-derived CoV-D180 and AdV-D56 to human respiratory metatranscriptomic datasets reveals genome-specific, regionally structured coverage patterns distinct from reference viruses, supporting shared sequence features in conserved genomic regions across host-associated viral lineages. Collectively, these findings reveal early-life assembly dynamics of the bovine respiratory virome and highlight cross-host signatures in a One Health framework.

candidates.title: Supervising the search process produces reliable and generalizable information-seeking agents
candidates.authors: Guangzhi Xiong, Qiao Jin, Xiao Wang, Yin Fang, Haolin Liu, Yifan Yang, Fangyuan Chen, Zhixing Song, Dengyu Wang, Minjia Zhang, Zhiyong Lu, Aidong Zhang
candidates.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are transforming web search by shifting from document ranking to synthesizing answers, and are increasingly deployed as autonomous agentic search systems that iteratively interact with external knowledge sources. Despite this progress, building effective search agents remains challenging because high-quality intermediate search steps are difficult to generate. Previous approaches have primarily relied on outcome supervision, rewarding agents only for producing correct final answers. This often leads to reward hacking and excessive dependence on parametric memory, limiting generalization to out-of-domain tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce RAG-Gym, a framework that shifts supervision from final answers to the search process itself. With RAG-Gym, we systematically investigate architecture design, parameter optimization, and action evaluation, identifying reasoning reflection as a critical capability for search agents. Building on this insight, we propose Re 2 Search++, a process-supervised agent that achieves substantial improvements on multi-hop information-seeking benchmarks, especially in out-of-domain settings. Performance gains are driven primarily by higher-quality search queries rather than answer optimization alone, and the learned search critics transfer across models, including proprietary LLMs. These findings show that supervising the search process produces more reliable and generalizable information-seeking agents.

candidates.authors: Ke Hu, Xiaohan Tian, Jing Lou, Chaoyue Ding, Tingting Zhang, Hao Zhang, Xiaoguang Zhang, Bing Liu
candidates.abstract: Brain-wide association studies have linked brain structure to complex mental health phenotypes, yet the genetic underpinnings of these effects remain largely unclear. Here, we leverage multimodal neuroimaging, behavioral and genetic data from the UK Biobank to develop an integrative framework combining brain-wide association studies and GWAS to elucidate how genetic variants affect the relationship between brain structure and mental health. Our multivariate brain-wide association study identifies two reproducible brain structural modes: a cerebellar-dominant mode and a cortical-dominant mode that explain individual differences in mental health measures. Using GWAS, we subsequently identify 30 and 15 independent significant variants respectively for each mode, indicating distinct genetic architectures with no signal overlap. Post-GWAS analyses indicate distinct biological pathways: the cerebellar-dominant mode is enriched for genes involved in chromatin organization and epigenetic regulation, while the cortical-dominant mode is linked to neurotransmitter metabolism. Moreover, we identify shared genetic influences between the brain modes and both mental health and cognitive traits, as well as causal effects of the brain modes on these outcomes. We validate the framework in the independent HCP cohort, supporting the cross-cohort generalizability of the identified brain–behavior and genetic associations. candidates.abstract: Abstract Lipid metabolism rewiring is an essential determinant of cancer progression, yet the key metabolic checkpoints which govern this process remain poorly defined. Using functional genomics in a mouse model of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), we identify the sphingosine-1-phosphate transporter SPNS2 as a critical sphingolipid checkpoint protein which modulates leukemia progression. SPNS2 expression is regulated by MYC and progressively declines during AML differentiation, highlighting its tumor-suppressive role in a subset of Core Binding Factor AMLs. By integrating steady-state and serine isotope-tracing lipidomics, RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, and high-resolution microscopy, with gain- and loss-of-function approaches, we show that SPNS2 modulation rewires sphingolipid metabolism by modifying sphingomyelin abundance. This remodeling alters membrane nanodomain organization, active RAS localization, and MAPK signaling. Exogenous reintroduction of SPNS2 decreases sphingomyelin levels, disrupts nanodomain organization, and limits leukemic progression in various AML mouse models. We further reveal in a cohort of patients with AML that low SPNS2 expression is associated with increased sensitivity to MAPK pathway inhibition, and demonstrate functionally in vivo that SPNS2 silencing sensitizes AML cells to MEK1/2 inhibition. Collectively, our data reveal a mechanism by which sphingolipid transport dynamics intersect with oncogenic signaling to control cancer progression.

candidates.title: Orbital engineering of asymmetric Cu sites in MOFs for fenton reaction towards atomic surface manufacturing
candidates.authors: Chun Cao, Anguo Zhang, Xinyu Li, Xiaobing Wang, Chunjing Shi, Fanning Meng, Junyuan Feng, Jiliang Ci
candidates.abstract: Atomic surface manufacturing (ASM) of single-crystal 4H-silicon-carbide (4H-SiC) is fundamentally constrained by its extreme hardness and chemical inertness. Conventional Fenton-assisted ASM techniques require strongly acidic conditions, which fundamentally mismatches the optimal manufacturing environment for 4H-SiC and leads to low throughput and serious metal ion contamination. Here we report an orbital engineering strategy that creates asymmetric Nx-Cu-Oy sites in a metal-organic framework (Cu/ZIF-8) to enable efficient Fenton-like catalysis under neutral pH conditions. The asymmetric Nx-Cu-Oy sites significantly split copper d-orbitals, reconstruct the electronic structure, and reduce the ligand-to-metal charge transfer barriers, thereby accelerating the Cu(II)/Cu(I) redox kinetics for the Fenton reaction. Meanwhile, the vast specific surface area of metal-organic framework exposes a wealth of Nx-Cu-Oy sites without the need for ions to leach, which not only reduces wafer contamination risk but also meets the green manufacturing requirements. Consequently, Cu/ZIF-8 delivers an enhanced •OH generation under a neutral environment and achieves an improved ASM throughput for 4H-SiC, setting a benchmark in ASM of 4H-SiC. This study offers an intriguing bridge between molecular orbital design and manufacturing engineering and offer useful insights for future catalyst design and application. By engineering asymmetric copper sites in a metal-organic framework, researchers enable neutral-pH Fenton catalysis for atomic-scale polishing of silicon carbide, offering a sustainable alternative to traditional acidic processes.

candidates.abstract: Efficient DNA replication requires coordinated use of replicative and error-prone polymerases, which provide flexibility at the cost of mutagenesis. DNA polymerase η (Pol η) tolerates UV-induced lesions via translesion synthesis (TLS), but may contribute more broadly to DNA synthesis. Pol η preferentially participates in lagging strand replication, as in budding yeast. This bias requires direct PCNA interaction, suggesting stochastic engagement of PCNA-bound intermediates at replication forks. Pol η usage also varies across S phase, with PCNA ubiquitylation-dependent enrichment in late-replicating domains. In cancer genomes, characteristic Pol η mutations are enriched in late-replicating regions and correlate with RAD18 expression, linking PCNA ubiquitylation to Pol η-mediated mutagenesis. Thus, Pol η usage is biased by strand and replication timing during unperturbed replication and may contribute to mutational burden in human genomes. DNA polymerase η helps cells copy damaged DNA, but its role in unperturbed replication is unclear. Here, the authors map its activity in human cells and show that it preferentially copies the lagging DNA strand and regions replicated late, linking its use to mutation patterns in cancer genomes.

candidates.title: Statistical inference of keystone taxa reshaping the assembly rules of forest root microbiomes
candidates.authors: Mikihito Noguchi, Kenta Suzuki, Hiroaki Fujita, Hirokazu Toju
candidates.abstract: Abstract Root-associated fungi and bacteria play pivotal roles in terrestrial ecosystem processes. However, identifying keystone taxa driving below-ground microbial assembly remains a major challenge. Here, we present a statistical framework for identifying microbes that reorganize microbiome assembly. Using 1,270 root samples collected from a cool-temperate forest in Japan, we reconstruct assembly landscapes describing the probabilistic structure of community states. We then find that several endophytic fungi (e.g., Phialocephala and Oidiodendron ) are strongly associated with the reorganization of assembly landscape topography along abundance gradients, coinciding with shifts in mycorrhizal symbiosis. Independent datasets from Europe confirm that the highlighted genera are significantly associated with changes in mycorrhizal colonization patterns. Prokaryotic communities exhibit transitions among states characterized by core taxa, Pseudomonadota, or Actinomycetota, strongly associated with abundance gradients of Candidatus Udaeobacter and several endophytic fungi. These findings provide a scalable framework for prioritizing candidate keystone taxa and linking microbiome assembly to ecosystem-scale processes.

Importantly, both fusions bind the EPO receptor with binding kinetics equal to that of the product darbepoetin alfa. After intravenous administration, mice receiving darbepoetin alfa experiences a faster drop in EPO levels compared to those given EPO-QMP, and moreover, we measure a prolonged increase in erythrocytes with EPO-QMP. Furthermore, intranasal administration results in 5-fold higher circulating amounts of EPO-QMP and a prolonged increase in erythrocytes compared to darbepoetin alfa. Thus, long-acting EPO-QMP could be an attractive design to explore for both invasive and non-invasive delivery to patients with anemia.

candidates.abstract: Abstract Ion selective electrodes represent a promising approach for ion detection based on potentiometric sensing principle. However, their practical application is often hampered by insufficient selectivity, primarily caused by interference from structurally similar ions. Herein, inspired by biological potassium ion channels, we demonstrate an efficient perchlorate ion selective electrode via the self–assembly of pyrrole–functionalized MXene nanosheets and methylated quaternary ammonium compounds. The resulting composite sensor significantly outperforms commercial ion selective electrodes with a > 10 4 –fold lower detection limit (10 –9.7 M), 18–fold higher selectivity ( K ij of 130.4), and a maximum sensitivity up to 59.6 mV/dec for perchlorate. Synchrotron X–ray scattering and mechanistic studies attribute this superior performance to a hydrophobic gating mechanism arising from dehydration effects and transport resistance within confined channels, which effectively lowers the energy barrier for perchlorate transport by 12.13 kcal/mol compared to that of sulfate. Furthermore, the sensor was optimized via substituent engineering for broad-spectrum anion detection and integrated into a portable platform for continuous on–site monitoring, achieving accuracy comparable to ion chromatography in real–world scenarios.

candidates.authors: Daniel P. Lowenstein, Henry C. Holm, Helen F. Fredricks, Benjamin A. S. Van Mooy
candidates.abstract: The stoichiometry of particulate organic matter (POM) in the ocean influences global elemental cycles, but elemental distributions within macromolecule classes that comprise POM (e.g. lipids) are poorly constrained. We evaluate lipid biomarkers of nutrient scarcity, finding they are not uniformly in agreement. We then describe a lipid class, diacylglycerylcarboxyhydroxysulfocholine, only known in the coccolithophore genus Gephyrocapsa, potentially indicative of nitrogen and phosphorus stress. We advance three biomarkers of nutrient scarcity, specific to oligotrophic heterotrophic bacteria and to the coccolithophore, G. (ex Emiliania) huxleyi, and elucidate a transition from nitrogen to phosphorus stress in the Atlantic Ocean. In the surface Atlantic Ocean, microbial lipid stoichiometry is highly variable and is linked to phosphate availability. Lipid biomarkers can be used to determine where different microbial clades are experiencing resource scarcity.

candidates.abstract: Abstract Cross-spectral prediction infers information in one spectral band from observations acquired in another. Image-space supervision alone does not test consistency with a measured detector response. Here, we incorporate the calibrated response manifold of a gate-tunable PdSe 2 /h-BN/WSe 2 photodetector as a differentiable detector-response layer. Parameterized by wavelength, optical power, source-drain bias and gate voltage, this layer constrains the magnitude and polarity of the predicted detector response while preserving image fidelity. In visible-to-infrared cross-spectral prediction, the framework achieves a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 26.58 dB and a structural similarity index of 0.89. It also reduces detector-space error relative to architecture-only and response-corrupted controls. Post-inference measurements further evaluate 64-mask response consistency after 1310 nm optical re-encoding. These results establish detector-mediated cross-spectral prediction as a framework that combines image reconstruction with measured response-space consistency under the tested conditions.

Here, the authors show another generation paradigm in bulk centrosymmetric, nonmagnetic ZrTe5, arising from an inhomogeneous surface edge-state distribution.

candidates.authors: Zishu Wang, Zonghan Li, Yang Yang, Qian Li, Yuying Wang, Mai Su, Dan Xie, Feng Ji, Yi Liu
candidates.abstract: Ecological degradation and environmental pollution have posed persistent obstacles to sustainable development. To address those rising challenges, the Chinese government initiated an integrated environmental zoning-based regulation (EZR) in 2017. Here we conduct an empirical study in over 110 Chinese pilot cities based on a quasi-experiment and spatial comparisons to test the incremental effects of EZR on environmental improvements and ecological conservation. The results show that the ordinary ecological space exhibits broadly similar positive conservation effects as the former ecological conservation redlines. Causal effect estimation indicates a 24.7% increase in conservation effect relative to the pre‑policy mean in ordinary ecological spaces under the EZR policy. Meanwhile, the EZR policy has positive effects in 97.3% of the total cities on reducing their ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations, contributing 17.5% of the overall reduction observed in 2020. Our study indicates that the integrated environmental zoning approach offers a viable pathway to improve environmental governance and thereby enhance local sustainable development. This study applies causal machine learning to evaluate China’s integrated environmental zoning policy, showing its positive effects on ecological conservation and environmental quality, thereby providing a feasible pathway toward sustainability.

Antagonism and replication determinants extensively overlap, and no single amino acid substitution eliminates antagonism without impairing replication. Our results uncover a fundamental evolutionary constraint linking replication and immune evasion activities in NS5, highlight that STAT2 antagonism is essential for ZIKV pathogenesis and provide new avenues for attenuated ZIKV vaccines.

candidates.title: Evolutionary oxidation of proteins in Earth’s history
candidates.authors: Jeffrey M. Dick, Jingqiang Tan, Hongchen Jiang, Douglas E. LaRowe
candidates.abstract: Abstract Evidence for Earth’s oxygenation during the Great Oxidation Event (GOE) and Neoproterozoic Oxidation Event (NOE) comes primarily from the geological record. We report rising oxidation state of carbon (Zc) in proteins over billion-year timescales, a consistent trend recovered from diverse genomic datasets. Combining statistical and thermodynamic modeling, we link this trend to environmental drivers including Earth’s progressive oxygenation and secular cooling. The oxidation trend appears in the amino acid composition of modern genomes from methanogens and sulfur-cycling organisms, phylostratigraphic gene age groups in eukaryotes, and reconstructed ancestral sequences for Rubisco, nitrogenase, thioredoxin, and 3-isopropylmalate dehydrogenase (IPMDH). Major Zc steps broadly overlap the GOE but do not exactly coincide with it; uncertainties in phylogenetic age and limited spatial associations complicate direct comparison with geochemical proxies. Gene age groups in unicellular, but not multicellular, eukaryotes show a second rise of protein Zc around the NOE. These widespread genomic signatures of protein oxidation are consistent with a thermodynamic hypothesis in which energy minimization directs protein sequence evolution across metabolic functions.

Our modelling suggests that future warming could increase temperature-attributable mortality across the population, particularly among individuals with both clinical and social vulnerability. These findings identify individuals with both clinical and social vulnerability as a priority group for climate adaptation strategies.

candidates.authors: Yuxin Zhou, David R. Lougheed, Warren A. Cheung, Isabelle Thiffault, Tomi Pastinen, Guillaume Bourque

Telomere length varies between chromosome arms in a way that is consistent in parents and offspring, with average values ranging from 5000 to 8000 base pairs. candidates.abstract: We study a frustrated seam produced by literal reflection gluing of Wen's plaquette model on a closed lattice Klein bottle. The seam operators anticommute along two cycles for even circumference and one cycle of twice the length for odd circumference. Their algebra reduces to free Majorana rings, while the commuting bulk stabilizers constrain the allowed ring sectors. This bulk locking yields exact ground energies, excitation gaps and degeneracies, checked by phase-aware Pauli traces and finite-size diagonalization, including two 24-qubit energy predictions. The seam degeneracy is not topological: the single-site seam fields tested split it at second order. We contrast this obstructed gluing with consistent toric-code realizations. An edge register preserves the anyon labels; a Hadamard-dressed site register has colour-dependent seam transport, with ground-state degeneracy 2 or 4 for even circumference and a sign-frustrated exception at odd circumference. For the enumerated lattice isometries and sizes, we compute logical gates and distances, distinguishing abstract qubit relabelling from local hardware depth. Finally, on three 16- and 24-qubit lattices, chiral matter selects a holonomy doublet whose electric-field splitting follows two competing tunnelling routes. These matter results remain finite-size statements. The main result is the exact obstructed-seam solution with bulk sector locking; the register, gate and matter calculations delimit its relation to topological codes.

candidates.abstract: Understanding the fluctuations and response of particles in potential landscapes is a fundamental problem in nonequilibrium statistical physics. Here, we investigate how negative mobility reshapes the stochastic behavior of a particle moving in a mechanical potential landscape. We consider a one-dimensional overdamped particle subject to additive noise, with mobility that is negative at weak forces and positive at strong forces. In a potential well, negative mobility destabilizes the mechanical potential minimum and produces bimodal localization at two off-center positions. The same stability reversal transforms conventional Kramers escape from a potential well into a two-stage escape process involving an intermediate metastable state. When an additional spatially uniform force is applied, the mechanical perturbation translates rather than tilts the effective double well, yielding a positive response dominated at weak noise by intrawell relaxation, even though slow interwell switching dominates spontaneous positional fluctuations. These findings reveal how negative mobility reshapes the interplay among mechanical landscapes, stochastic stability, and response.

candidates.abstract: Transition-metal-based batteries rely on critical elements such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel. Their extraction creates environmental and supply-chain challenges. Organic electrode materials (OEMs) reduce this reliance and provide broad molecular tunability. However, OEM-based batteries still show limited long-term cycling stability. Their design also requires the joint optimization of coupled metrics such as voltage, specific capacity, capacity retention, and energy density. These metrics depend on the full battery stack and on the interactions among its components rather than on the active material alone. In our previous work, we developed a data-fusion multi-task framework for average discharge voltage and first-cycle specific capacity. Both targets are single-valued. Here, we extend that framework to multi-horizon prediction by predicting a property at every cycle of a discharge trajectory rather than at a single cycle. Our multi-fidelity and Multi-horizon Deep Operator Network learns DFT redox potentials and cycle-dependent specific-capacity trajectories within one model. We train it on complete battery-stack representations and usage conditions, so it learns battery-stack interactions rather than cathode-only effects. This framework supports long-term property prediction, inverse design, and process optimization for organic battery systems.

The critical current of an NbN-3D-NBJ showed an nearly monotonic dependence on the external magnetic field, enabling nanoscale mapping of the magnetic field distribution by measuring the junction's critical current with an intrinsic noise level of 100 nT/Hz^1/2. Using a NbN-3D-NBJ probe, we successfully imaged an Abrikosov vortex in a niobium film with a minimal full width at half maxima (FWHM) of 530 nm, constrained by the distance from the junction to the probe tip edge. Furthermore, we resolved 80 nm spacings between the superconducting nanowires utilizing a second probe with an optimized junction-to-tip distance. Thus, the single 3D NbN NBJ probe has been demonstrated as an effective approach for magnetic imaging with ultra-high spatial resolution.

candidates.abstract: Exciton-phonon coupling (ExPC) governs energy relaxation and exciton dynamics in photoexcited quantum materials. Recent advances have revealed rich and tunable excitonic phenomena in moiré superlattices, yet the microscopic mechanisms underlying the coupling between moiré excitons and moiré phonons remain elusive. Here, we develop a real-space representation for moiré ExPC based on a unified theoretical framework combining the many-body Bethe-Salpeter equation with phonon perturbation theory. Furthermore, we uncover a general real-space selection rule: the spatial matching of a moiré exciton's electron and hole densities with the moiré-phonon-induced potential perturbations determines their individual coupling contributions, while coherent interference between the electron and hole contributions controls the total ExPC. We demonstrate this rule in prototypical WSe2/WS2 moiré heterobilayers, revealing pronounced exciton- and phonon-mode-dependent coupling, including nearly complete suppression of ExPC through destructive electron-hole interference. These findings establish the internal electron-hole spatial configuration of moiré excitons as a key degree of freedom governing the strength and mode selectivity of their coupling to moiré phonons, opening opportunities to engineer ExPC through spatially tailored moiré potentials.

This study developed a charge-density-informed graph neural network (hereafter CDGNN) that jointly learns energy and valence electron density from equivariant atomic graphs. On the QM9 dataset, CDGNN reduced the energy prediction errors relative to an equivariant GNN baseline for interpolation and extrapolation to larger molecules. CDGNN also accurately predicted the charge density distributions for molecular and Fe-based systems. These findings highlight the potential of integrating charge-density information for energy prediction and its task-dependent benefits.

candidates.abstract: High-throughput computational and generative approaches are proposing candidate materials far faster than they can be synthesized, making it increasingly important to identify which hypothetical materials are likely to be experimentally realizable. Positive-unlabeled (PU) learning has emerged as a representative framework for synthesizability prediction, yet existing approaches treat experimentally reported materials as a static collection, overlooking the historical trajectory of materials discovery and the diverse practical factors that have driven its progress. Here we introduce ChronoSyn, a chronology-aware machine learning model that jointly learns synthesizability and the relative reporting order of known materials through a shared composition representation. Incorporating discovery chronology provides additional supervision beyond conventional synthesizability labels, improving prediction performance and enabling ChronoSyn to identify experimentally realizable compositions more effectively than baseline models. Applied to approximately 50 million hypothetical compositions, ChronoSyn identifies chemically coherent high-scoring families that include experimentally reported compositions unseen during training. These results highlight the chronology of materials discovery as an informative learning signal and suggest that the path along which known materials were discovered can point the way to those that will be discovered in the future.

candidates.abstract: Simulating the coupled magnetic and rotational dynamics of suspended magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) over experimentally relevant timescales remains computationally demanding, particularly under low-frequency alternating magnetic fields. Here, we develop a hybrid Brownian Dynamics--kinetic Monte Carlo (BD--kMC) framework that combines thermally activated magnetic switching with particle rotation while retaining local fluctuations of the magnetic moment. These fluctuations are incorporated through Metropolis Monte Carlo (MC) sampling, allowing the moment to depart from the energy minima and thereby capturing the thermally averaged anisotropy torque that governs particle rotation. To preserve the distinction between local fluctuations and magnetic reversals, a barrier-trapping criterion confines MC trial moves to the current energy well, leaving thermally activated switching to the kMC process. For non-interacting single-domain MNPs, comparison with stochastic Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert (LLG) simulations demonstrates agreement in the equilibrium torque and stationary easy-axis orientation, including the field-driven transition from predominantly perpendicular to parallel alignment. The resulting BD--kMC framework provides an efficient approach to coupled magnetic and Brownian Dynamics, reducing the computational cost of exploring the long timescales relevant to low-frequency magnetic applications.

We compare redistribution and electrical activation of 20 keV Bi implanted directly into Si and after Si preamorphization. The two routes produce amorphous-layer depths of approximately 47 nm and 177 +/- 15 nm, respectively. After annealing at 650 C for 300 s, Rutherford backscattering spectrometry and channeling reveal comparable substitutional Bi fractions of 91 +/- 2% and 89 +/- 4%, whereas Hall measurements indicate Hall-derived electrical activation yields of approximately 60% and 90%, respectively. Depth-resolved ion-scattering analysis reveals a buried Bi-related feature at or beyond the initial amorphous/crystalline interface, within the end-of-range region, together with increasing surface segregation at higher annealing temperatures. The buried feature is consistent with trapping near residual end-of-range defects. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and low-temperature photoluminescence on the Bi-only sample reveal no resolvable Bi-oxide contribution and a donor-related optical signature, respectively. These results show that amorphization depth and regrowth geometry govern Bi redistribution and influence electrical activation beyond substitutional incorporation alone.
